B.105.notes: Heading (the editor's): 'COURTAUDS POUR NAVIRES'. The only text on the page belongs to the lower drawing, the long curved blade, which the curator's reason calls 'a hinged scoop'; text and edition make it a scythe to be fired from ships. The revolving crane, the curator's lead drawing, has no text on this page, so 'lead' is null. Checked on the edition's plate (Polona scan 200).

it.text: — questi ~~bo~~ chortaldi deono stare sopra forti navili equesti 2 chortaldi arano con forte chatena o corda nova bagniata vna falce lunga braccia 12 larga nel mezo uno pie grssa [grossa] nella costa uno dito e debesidare focho invno tenpo

en.text: These short cannons must stand on strong ships, and these 2 short cannons shall have, on a strong chain or a new wet rope, a scythe 12 braccia long, one foot wide in the middle, one finger thick at the back; and they must be fired at the same moment.
en.label: Translated by AI from the printed text of Charles Ravaisson-Mollien, 1881 to 1891. It may contain errors.
doubts: 'chortaldi' (cortaldi, French 'courtauds') are short, wide-bored cannons; 'short cannons' is a plain gloss.
'arano con forte chatena ... vna falce' is read as the scythe being fastened to the guns by the chain or rope; the Italian only says the guns 'shall have, with a strong chain or rope, a scythe'.
The struck-out 'bo' (italics in the edition) is left out; 'grssa [grossa]' follows the editor's bracket.

The facing page, fol. 36 recto (next leaf, heading [CONSTRUCTION]), carries 'il tetto eposato sulla rota' (Le toit est posé sur la roue: the roof rests on the wheel), which belongs to the same windmill idea but is not on this page. On the edition's plate the last line stands by the digging men, so it is the lead; that placement is read from the plate, not stated by the edition.
